BootPass.definition: A movement passing concept in which the quarterback presents a run-action fake to the running back, keeps the ball, and moves away from the apparent run direction toward the opposite edge. The quarterback gains width and depth outside or near the original pocket while receivers execute coordinated crossing, flat, intermediate, and deep routes designed to create layered passing options.

QB opens toward the running back immediately after receiving the snap
QB extends the ball and presents a visible handoff or mesh action
RB continues through the apparent run track after the quarterback keeps the ball
Offensive linemen step or block in the direction of the apparent run action
QB pulls the ball and moves away from the direction of the run fake
QB reverses out or continues behind the line toward the opposite edge
QB gains lateral width and depth outside or near the boundary of the original pocket
QB turns the shoulders and attention downfield while continuing the designed movement
At least one eligible receiver crosses the formation at shallow or intermediate depth
A flat receiver delays or crosses behind the formation before releasing toward the quarterback's movement side
An intermediate receiver runs an over, cross, corner, comeback, or similar route into the boot side
A deep receiver runs a vertical or clear-out route above the intermediate route
A slicing blocker may cross behind the line to seal or influence the backside edge
QB sets, resets, or throws while outside or near the edge of the original pocket
The run fake, opposite-direction quarterback movement, and coordinated route structure develop as one designed sequence
BootPass.notes: The defining sequence is a visible run-action fake, the quarterback pulling the ball and moving away from the apparent run direction, designed width outside or near the original pocket, and coordinated passing routes developing with the movement. Open To Running Back, Fake Handoff, Pull Ball, Boot Away, and Gain Width are defining quarterback actions. Run Mesh Track and Sell Run are defining running-back actions. Cross Formation by an eligible receiver is a strong route cue, while the exact flat, intermediate, and deep route combination may vary. Zone Block represents the initial run-direction blocking behavior but may be replaced by Reach Block, Down Block, Cutoff Block, or another scheme-specific action. Escape Pocket is designed movement in this context and should not automatically be classified as a scramble. Reset To Throw, Catch Pass, Secure Catch, Turn Upfield, Run After Catch, and Ball Carry are optional outcomes. Do not classify a standard dropback pass, pocket play action, sprint-out pass, quarterback keeper, or pressure-induced rollout as Boot Pass unless the run fake, opposite-direction boot movement, and coordinated route structure are reasonably visible.

Counter.definition: A gap-scheme misdirection run featuring playside down blocks and two backside pullers—one to kick out the edge defender and one to lead through the hole. The running back takes an initial false step away before cutting back to follow the pullers.
observable_cues: RB fakes a step toward the play-side
Backside OG aligned slightly off-tackle pre-snap
Offensive line shows inside/down-block angles at snap
QB pivots sharply away from fake at mesh point

player_actions.notes: Exploits defensive aggression and over-pursuit; timing between fake and pull is critical; vulnerable if backside pursuit maintains leverage.

Cover1.definition: A man-coverage defense in which underneath defenders are assigned to eligible receivers while one deep safety protects the middle of the field. Cornerbacks, linebackers, nickel defenders, and safeties maintain identifiable receiver relationships through releases, route stems, breaks, and extended-play movement. The post safety gains depth, reads the quarterback, and provides help against vertical routes, while an additional defender may occupy a low-hole, rat, or robber responsibility. Cover 1 may be paired with a standard pass rush or additional blitzers, and its identification depends on the post-snap man assignments and single-high safety structure rather than the result of the play.
Cover1.coverage_structure: Cover 1 uses one primary deep-middle defender, usually a safety aligned in the post before the snap or rotating there immediately afterward. The remaining coverage defenders match eligible receivers in man coverage. Cornerbacks commonly handle outside wide receivers, nickel or dime defenders cover slot receivers, and linebackers or safeties may match tight ends and running backs. Underneath defenders use leverage based on the location of available help, often funneling routes toward the post safety or an underneath helper. Man defenders carry receivers through vertical stems, follow crossing routes, and remain connected through route breaks rather than passing receivers between fixed zones. Against motion, bunches, stacks, and switch releases, defenders may travel, communicate, or exchange assignments while preserving the overall man-coverage structure. A second safety or linebacker may rotate into the low hole or robber area to help against in-breaking routes, crossing routes, or quarterback movement. The structure differs from Cover 0 because Cover 1 retains a dedicated deep-middle safety, from Cover 3 because the underneath defenders play man rather than distributing routes through zones, from Cover 2 because there are not two deep-half defenders, and from Cover 4 because there are not four deep-quarter defenders.

Cover1.notes: Cover 1 should be identified from post-snap evidence of one deep-middle safety and multiple underneath man-coverage relationships. A single-high pre-snap alignment alone is insufficient because Cover 3 and other rotations may present a similar shell. Motion may support a man-coverage diagnosis, but travel with motion is not conclusive without matching post-snap behavior. Assignment exchanges against bunches or stacks do not automatically make the coverage zone if defenders continue with identifiable man responsibilities after the exchange. Poor execution, lost leverage, or separation by a receiver does not change the intended coverage when the original assignment remains visible. Low-hole, robber, press, trail, bracket, and blitz variations should be assigned only when clearly supported by the clip. Because no specific video evidence is provided here, this definition uses broad Cover 1 actions and does not identify a particular variation, matchup, pressure, coverage bust, or play result.

Cover2.definition: A two-deep zone coverage in which two safeties divide the deep field into left and right halves while cornerbacks and underneath defenders protect the flats, curls, hooks, seams, and middle zones. The safeties maintain depth and leverage over vertical routes, cornerbacks reroute or pass outside receivers before settling into short outside responsibilities, and linebackers or nickel defenders distribute receiving threats through the underneath zones. Cover 2 is identified from the post-snap two-deep structure and zone-based route distribution rather than the result of the play.
Cover2.coverage_structure: Cover 2 uses two deep safeties, with each safety responsible for approximately one half of the deep field. The safeties gain depth and width after the snap, remain over the top of vertical routes, and overlap receiving threats entering their halves. Cornerbacks generally align over the outside receivers, disrupt or influence releases when possible, and remain responsible for the short outside or flat areas rather than carrying receivers through the entire deep field. Linebackers, nickel defenders, and other underneath defenders divide the hook, curl, seam, and middle zones while reading the quarterback and relating to receivers entering their areas. Underneath defenders may carry vertical routes temporarily, reroute inside releases, and pass receivers to adjacent defenders or deep safeties. Crossing routes are distributed between zones rather than followed continuously by one defender. Cover 2 differs from Cover 1 because it uses zone coverage underneath instead of man assignments, from Cover 3 because it has two deep-half defenders instead of three deep-zone defenders, from Cover 4 because the cornerbacks remain underneath rather than protecting deep quarters, and from Two-Man because the underneath defenders protect zones rather than following individual receivers.

A two-high pre-snap shell alone is insufficient because the defense may rotate into Cover 1, Cover 3, Cover 4, Two-Man, or a split-field coverage. Briefly carrying or matching a receiver does not automatically indicate man coverage when the defender ultimately transfers the route and returns to a zone responsibility. Tampa 2 should be assigned only when a middle defender clearly gains substantial vertical depth between the safeties. Trap, cloud, pattern-match, and zone-pressure variations should be identified only when clearly visible. Poor execution, a missed handoff, or a defender leaving a zone does not change the intended coverage when the original responsibility remains observable. Because no specific video evidence is provided here, this definition uses broad Cover 2 responsibilities and does not identify a particular variation, pressure, coverage bust, matchup, or play result.

Cover3.definition: A three-deep zone coverage in which one defender protects the deep middle third and two defenders protect the deep outside thirds. Underneath defenders distribute short-to-intermediate threats through curl-flat, hook, seam, and middle zones while reading the quarterback and maintaining spacing between receivers. Cover 3 may be executed as spot-drop or pattern-match coverage and may include sky, buzz, cloud, robber, or zone-pressure variations. The coverage is identified from the post-snap three-deep structure and zone-based route distribution rather than the result of the play.
Cover3.coverage_structure: Cover 3 divides the deep field among one deep-middle safety and two outside-third defenders, typically cornerbacks. The deep-middle safety gains depth and remains between central vertical threats, while the outside-third defenders protect the deep sidelines and stay over the top of outside vertical routes. Four underneath defenders commonly divide the curl-flat, hook, seam, and middle areas. Curl-flat defenders widen with outside releases while maintaining sufficient depth beneath deeper routes. Hook and seam defenders protect interior throwing lanes, carry vertical releases when necessary, and pass crossing or in-breaking routes to adjacent defenders. Cornerbacks may use press-bail, off-zone, or pattern-match technique before settling into their outside-third responsibilities. A safety, nickel defender, or linebacker may rotate downward into an underneath zone, and the defense may rotate from a two-high pre-snap shell into a single-high, three-deep structure. Pattern-match variations may create temporary man-like relationships, but the overall defense retains three deep-zone defenders and underneath route distribution.

Cover3.notes: Cover 3 should be identified from post-snap evidence of one deep-middle defender, two outside-third defenders, and underneath zone distribution. A single-high pre-snap shell alone is insufficient because Cover 1 may present a similar alignment. Cornerbacks gaining depth into outside thirds and underneath defenders passing receivers through zones are important distinguishing cues. A defender briefly carrying or matching a receiver does not automatically indicate man coverage when the overall structure remains three deep. Sky, buzz, cloud, robber, match, and fire-zone variations should be assigned only when their corresponding rotations or responsibilities are clearly visible. Poor execution, missed route handoffs, or vacated zones do not automatically change the intended coverage when the original responsibilities remain observable. Cover4.definition: A four-deep coverage in which two cornerbacks protect the outside deep quarters and two safeties protect the inside deep quarters. Underneath defenders distribute curl, hook, seam, and flat threats while the quarter defenders maintain deep leverage, read receiver releases, and carry, match, overlap, or pass off vertical routes according to the coverage rules. Safeties may trigger downhill when their keyed receiver no longer threatens vertically. Cover 4 is identified from the post-snap four-deep structure and quarter-based route distribution rather than the result of the play.
Cover4.coverage_structure: Cover 4 divides the deep field among four defenders: two outside-quarter defenders and two inside-quarter safeties. The cornerbacks gain or maintain depth over outside vertical threats while protecting the deep sidelines. The safeties align or rotate into positions over the inside receiving threats and protect the deep inside quarters. Each safety reads the release of a slot receiver, tight end, or another inside threat and may carry a vertical route, overlap a route entering the quarter, exchange responsibility according to the route combination, or trigger downhill when no vertical threat remains. Underneath defenders divide the curl-flat, hook, seam, and middle areas while reading the quarterback and maintaining spacing between receiving threats. Pattern-match variations may create sustained man-like relationships, but the defense remains organized around four deep-quarter responsibilities. Against motion, bunches, stacks, trips, and switch releases, defenders may adjust leverage, communicate, carry receivers, pass routes, switch assignments, or poach threats from another coverage area.

Cover6.definition: A split-field defensive coverage that combines Cover 4 or quarters principles on one side of the formation with Cover 2 principles on the opposite side. The quarters side uses one cornerback to protect the outside deep quarter and one safety to protect the inside deep quarter, while the Cover 2 side uses one safety to protect the deep half and one cornerback or outside defender to protect the flat. Underneath defenders distribute hook, curl, seam, and flat threats according to the side-specific coverage rules. Cover 6 is identified from its asymmetrical quarter-quarter-half structure and post-snap route distribution rather than the outcome of the play.
Cover6.coverage_structure: Cover 6 divides the field into a quarters side and a Cover 2 side. On the quarters side, the cornerback gains depth into the outside quarter and carries or matches an outside vertical receiver, while the safety protects the inside quarter and reads the release of the slot receiver, tight end, or another inside threat. On the Cover 2 side, the safety gains width and depth into a deep-half responsibility while the cornerback remains underneath, reroutes the outside receiver, protects the flat, sinks beneath deeper outside routes, or passes a vertical threat to the safety. Underneath defenders distribute curl-flat, hook, seam, and middle threats differently on each side. The asymmetrical structure commonly produces three primary deep defenders but differs from Cover 3 because it does not use a single deep-middle defender with two outside thirds. Motion, bunches, stacks, trips, compressed formations, and switch releases may cause defenders to reset leverage, communicate, exchange assignments, or adjust which side uses quarters and which side uses Cover 2 principles.

Cover6.notes: Cover 6 should be identified from post-snap evidence of quarter responsibilities on one side and Cover 2 responsibilities on the opposite side. A two-high pre-snap shell alone is insufficient because Cover 2, Cover 4, Two-Man, and other split-field coverages may present similar alignments. The most important distinguishing evidence is the asymmetrical behavior of the cornerbacks and safeties: one cornerback gains depth into an outside quarter while the opposite cornerback remains underneath, and one safety protects an inside quarter while the opposite safety protects a deep half. Three deep defenders alone do not establish Cover 6 because Cover 3 also uses three deep defenders but distributes them into thirds from a single-high structure. Do not assume which side is the quarters side based only on formation strength, field position, or receiver count. Palms, poach, bracket, trap, cloud, match, and reversed Cover 6 variations should be assigned only when clearly visible. Poor execution, missed handoffs, or lost leverage do not automatically change the intended coverage when the original split-field responsibilities remain observable. Because no specific video evidence is provided here, this definition uses broad Cover 6 responsibilities and does not identify a particular variation, side designation, coverage check, pressure, bust, matchup, or play result.

CrackToss.definition: Gap scheme with playside down blocks and a crack block from the backside receiver to seal the defensive end, optionally with a backside guard pull

CrackToss.notes: Effective against aggressive inside-fit defenses; requires precise timing between toss and crack block; vulnerable to backside pursuit if seal fails.

Dagger.definition: A dropback passing concept where an inside receiver runs a vertical clear-out route to occupy or remove the middle-field defender while an outside receiver pushes vertically before breaking inside on a deep dig route, attacking the vacated intermediate middle of the field.

Dagger.notes: The defining feature is the layered vertical-and-dig combination, with the inside receiver clearing the middle and the outside receiver entering the vacated intermediate window. The concept is commonly used against single-high and split-safety coverages, but route depth and timing may vary by formation, coverage, and protection.

DeepCross.definition: A deep passing concept in which the primary receiver releases vertically or on an angled stem, gains more than 25 yards of depth beyond the line of scrimmage, and then bends or breaks across the field toward the opposite sideline. The receiver maintains speed through the crossing path while the quarterback uses extended timing, sustained protection, play action, rollout movement, or a deeper pocket set to deliver the ball into the deep crossing window.

DeepCross.notes: The defining sequence is a sustained vertical or angled stem, more than 25 yards of depth measured from the line of scrimmage, a bend or break across the field, and continued speed through a long field-spanning crossing path. Either Vertical Stem or Angled Stem may establish the route, and either Bend Across Field or Break Across Field may define the transition into the cross. Visible field markings and player movement should be used to estimate route depth when exact coordinates are unavailable. Play Action, Roll Out, Escape Pocket, and Step Up In Pocket are optional quarterback actions. Track Ball, Catch Pass, Secure Catch, Turn Upfield, and Run After Catch are optional outcomes. The route may still qualify if the pass is thrown before the receiver completes the full crossing path, provided the receiver has already exceeded 25 yards of depth and clearly begun the deep cross. Do not label a shallow cross, drag, standard over route, dig, post, glance, or slant as Deep Cross unless the receiver gains substantial depth and crosses a large portion of the field.

Draw.definition: A deceptive delayed run where the quarterback sells a pass drop before handing off to the running back, exploiting defenders who vacate interior gaps, then the RB cuts upfield through seams created by zone-down blocks.
observable_cues: Offensive line initially pass-sets (flat kick-slide)

Linebackers flow up anticipating pass, opening A-gaps
Draw.notes: Most effective versus aggressive four-man rushes; key is timing between QB sell and RB mesh; susceptible to quick-fitting linebackers if seal fails.

Duo.definition: A downhill interior run built around multiple adjacent double teams on interior defensive linemen, with offensive linemen working vertically to create displacement before one blocker releases to the second level based on linebacker movement. The running back presses an interior track, reads the leverage of a designated linebacker, and makes a decisive cut through the resulting A-gap or B-gap. Duo can resemble Inside Zone, but it uses a more vertical, gap-oriented blocking structure and normally does not require a pulling offensive lineman.

Duo.notes: Duo is distinguished from Inside Zone by its vertical displacement, multiple interior double teams, and limited lateral stretch; Inside Zone generally uses more coordinated lateral zone steps and covered-uncovered blocking rules. Unlike Power or Counter, base Duo normally has no pulling offensive lineman. Unlike Iso, Duo is built around multiple offensive-line double teams rather than primarily isolating one linebacker with a fullback. The RB commonly reads a designated linebacker instead of immediately selecting the first open gap. Exact double-team combinations and second-level releases change according to the defensive front.

FieldGoalBlock.definition: A special-teams play in which the defensive field-goal block unit penetrates or elevates through the protection and makes visible contact with the kicked ball at or near the kick point, altering its normal trajectory and potentially creating a dead-ball result, loose-ball recovery, or return opportunity.
