FieldGoalBlock.notes: Field-goal blocks may result from interior-gap pressure, edge pressure, A-gap or B-gap overloads, leverage techniques, push-pull techniques, or other overload structures. The block may be made by an interior rusher, edge rusher, leverage player, or another defender who reaches the kick point. Low-trajectory kicks are more vulnerable to blocks, but a low kick without visible or strongly supported defender contact should not automatically be classified as blocked. Attempt Block records a directed jump, dive, reach, or arm extension toward the kicked ball, while Block Kick requires visible or strongly supported defender-to-ball contact. Deflect Ball requires an observable trajectory change caused by that contact. Defender contact may occur with a hand, arm, helmet, shoulder, or another body part. Partial deflections may still allow the ball to travel forward or even approach the uprights, while stronger blocks may send the ball backward, sideways, downward, upward, or directly into the line. Pressure, penetration, jumping, arm extension, a missed kick, or contact with the kicker after the ball is away is not sufficient by itself. A bad snap or failed hold is not a Field Goal Block unless the ball is placed, kicked, and contacted by a defender. Blocked kicks may become dead immediately or remain live depending on the situation, but live-ball status should not be inferred when it cannot be visually confirmed. Either team may recover the ball, and a recovery may lead to a return, tackle, out-of-bounds result, or pileup. Attempt Recovery identifies a reach, bend, dive, fall, or competition for the ball, while Secure Recovery requires visible possession and control. Diving onto or reaching toward the ball does not prove recovery. Pileups may obscure possession, and camera views may temporarily lose the ball at the kick point, making contact or the exact deflection frame difficult to determine. Penalties may affect the result without being visible in the clip. Field Goal Block should be distinguished from Made Field Goal, Missed Field Goal, Bad Snap, Failed Hold, Field Goal Pressure, Blocked Extra Point, Fake Field Goal, and a loose-ball recovery not caused by defender contact with the kicked ball.

Hitch.definition: A short passing concept in which the primary receiver releases vertically for a brief distance, rapidly decelerates, plants, and turns back toward the quarterback to present a stationary or nearly stationary target. The quarterback uses a quick drop or catch-and-throw rhythm and delivers the pass as the receiver completes the turn and settles in open space.
observable_cues: Primary receiver aligns outside, in the slot, or as an attached receiving threat with space to run a short vertical stem
Primary receiver releases vertically and initially threatens continued movement upfield
Primary receiver maintains a short vertical stem before beginning the route break
Primary receiver rapidly reduces speed at shallow or intermediate route depth
Primary receiver sinks the hips and stops forward momentum
Primary receiver plants and turns the shoulders and head toward the quarterback
Primary receiver settles in place or takes only a small number of steps back toward the quarterback
Primary receiver presents a stationary or nearly stationary target
QB executes a quick pass drop or catch-and-throw action
QB sets and delivers a short pass near the receiver's turn
Offensive line uses quick pass sets and maintains short-duration pass protection
RB checks protection before blocking, releasing into the flat, or providing a checkdown option
Complementary receivers run vertical, clear-out, flat, slant, underneath, or backside routes to occupy nearby defenders
Hitch.notes: The defining sequence is the primary receiver's short vertical stem, rapid deceleration, plant and stop, turn toward the quarterback, and settlement as a short stationary target. Sink Hips and Present Target strengthen identification but may not be clearly visible in every clip. Track Ball, Catch Pass, Secure Catch, Turn Upfield, and Run After Catch are optional outcomes and should not be required for classification. Do not label a curl, comeback, Stop and Go, quick out, or slant as Hitch unless the receiver clearly stops forward momentum and turns toward the quarterback after a short vertical stem.

InsideZoneRead.definition: Zone-blocking scheme where the offensive line executes inside-zone steps while the quarterback reads an unblocked defender to decide whether to hand off to the running back or keep the ball and run.
observable_cues: Interior linemen step laterally in unison
RB aligned next to QB in shotgun
Mesh-point exchange between QB and RB
QB reads unblocked defender (DE/LB)
Defender hesitation or crash at line
InsideZoneRead.notes: Stresses inside-fit defenders; requires disciplined OL lateral movement and precise timing at the mesh point; vulnerable to backside pursuit if seal breaks.

InsideZoneStretch.definition: A zone-blocking inside run in which the back takes a lateral “stretch” step before choosing a cut-up lane through the OL’s zone blocks.
observable_cues: Offensive line steps laterally toward play side at snap
Quarterback delivers quick handoff
Running back’s first step is a stretch step toward the edge
Defensive end and linebackers flow laterally with the stretch action
InsideZoneStretch.notes: Effective to exploit aggressive inside fits; requires linemen to sustain blocks at the second level; vulnerable to defensive line penetration or backside pursuit. The inside zone stretch aims for vertical displacement, with the running back pressing for an internal cutback lane. The outside zone stretch, however, works to stretch the defense horizontally, with the back looking to attack the perimeter.

Iso.definition: An inside gap run where the fullback leads through the B-gap to isolate the play-side linebacker, clearing a single-block path for the ball carrier.
observable_cues: FB aligned directly behind QB in an I-set
PS OG shows a down-block angle toward the defensive tackle
BS OG (or C) pulls and leads through the PS B-gap
FB’s eyes/head up on MIKE/LB pre-snap
At snap: QB pivots and hands off inside
RB cuts to B-gap following FB
Iso.notes: Fundamental play at all levels; excels vs. 4-3 under and wide fronts. Vulnerable to backside pursuit and LB stunts if lead block misses.

JetSweep.definition: A speed-sweep action where a motion man (typically a receiver) takes a handoff or pitch from the QB and attacks the edge in a zone-blocking scheme.
observable_cues: Pre-snap jet motion by WR
Offensive line zone blocks to playside
QB quick pivot and pitch
Receiver hugs formation then bursts upfield
JetSweep.notes: Effective at stressing perimeter defenses; requires precise timing; vulnerable to backside pursuit.

KickoffReturnTouchdown.definition: A special-teams scoring play in which the receiving team fields a kickoff, establishes possession, executes a coordinated return and blocking scheme, and advances the ball into the opponent's end zone while maintaining control.
observable_cues: Kicking team aligns in a standard kickoff formation
Return team is distributed across front-line, second-level, and deep-return positions
Kicker approaches and kicks the ball deep, directionally, or on a squib trajectory
Returner tracks the ball and adjusts toward its projected landing point
Returner catches an airborne kick or collects a bouncing, rolling, or loose ball
Returner secures the ball against the hands, arm, chest, or body before advancing
Return-unit players retreat, turn, or reposition to establish blocking leverage
Front-line and second-level blockers identify approaching coverage players
Blockers engage, screen, seal, or redirect coverage players away from the return lane
Returner presses the designed return lane while reading the developing blocks
Lead blockers advance ahead of the returner through the return path
Returner follows blocks and accelerates through an available crease
Returner makes one or more cuts or changes direction to avoid defenders
Returner breaks, slips, or avoids tackle attempts while maintaining balance and possession
Coverage players pursue the returner from inside-out, outside-in, or from behind
Returner reaches open field and continues advancing toward the opponent's end zone
Teammates escort the returner and remain positioned to block pursuing defenders
Returner visibly crosses the opponent's goal line while controlling the ball
End-zone possession, an official touchdown signal, or other reliable visual evidence confirms the score
Play ends after the touchdown, official signal, celebration, or whistle
KickoffReturnTouchdown.notes: Kickoff return touchdowns may develop from middle, boundary, field, cross-field, or wedge return schemes and may occur against deep, directional, squib, or short kicks. Catch Kick applies only when the returner cleanly receives an airborne kickoff, while Collect Ball applies when possession is gained from a bouncing, rolling, muffed, or loose ball. Secure Ball requires visible control and must not be inferred from brief contact with the football. Press Return Lane identifies the returner's initial attack of the designed path, Follow Block identifies movement behind a blocker using that block's leverage, and Cut To Lane identifies a plant and redirection into an available crease. Break Tackle requires meaningful defender contact followed by continued advancement, while Avoid Tackle applies when the returner evades the attempt without being significantly controlled. Miss Tackle should only be assigned when an observable tackle attempt fails. Returns may include multiple cuts, reversals of field, broken tackles, missed tackles, laterals, or handoffs during unusual designed returns. Cross Goal Line requires the ball carrier to visibly cross the opponent's goal line while maintaining control, and Touchdown requires reliable scoring evidence such as visible end-zone entry, continued possession in the end zone, an official signal, or scoreboard confirmation. Significant yardage, celebration, reduced pursuit, the returner leaving the camera view, or a clip ending near the goal line is not sufficient by itself. Penalties may nullify an apparent touchdown without being visible in the clip, and some camera views may temporarily lose the returner or ball, making possession or the exact goal-line crossing frame uncertain. A true kickoff return touchdown should be distinguished from a recovery touchdown that occurs after a muff, fumble, or extended loose-ball sequence.

OnsideKickRecovery.definition: A special-teams recovery play in which the receiving team uses a hands-team alignment and coordinated recovery technique to secure a deliberately short kickoff after the ball becomes legally recoverable, while nearby teammates screen or block coverage players away from the recovery point.
observable_cues: Receiving team aligns multiple players near the restraining line instead of using a normal deep-return structure
Front-line receivers use upright or staggered ready stances with their eyes directed toward the kicker and ball
Kicker approaches and strikes the top, side, or lower portion of the ball to create a short recovery trajectory
Ball travels on a short, low, bouncing, rolling, or high-hop path rather than a normal deep kickoff
Front-line receiving players track the ball and hold their depth instead of immediately retreating to set up a return
Receiving players may wait for the ball to cross the legal recovery distance or for another player to touch it before attempting recovery
A designated hands player advances toward the projected recovery point
Nearby receiving players block or screen coverage players away from the ball
Recovering player bends, kneels, dives, falls, or reaches toward the loose ball
Successful recovery is shown by the player securing and controlling the ball against the hands, chest, or ground
Nearby teammates close around and protect the recovering player after possession is established
Coverage players contest the recovery point, attempt a tackle, or join a developing pile
Play ends with a tackle, pileup, official signal, or whistle
OnsideKickRecovery.notes: Common variations include traditional bouncing onside kicks, rolling kicks, high-hop or pop-up kicks, and surprise onside kicks from a standard kickoff alignment. Attempt Recovery identifies a player reaching, bending, kneeling, or diving toward the loose ball, but does not indicate possession. Dive For Ball records the body action only and must not be treated as a successful recovery. Secure Recovery requires visible possession and control of the ball, while Cover Ball describes protecting the ball after control is established. Block Coverage Player and Screen Defender are separate from recovery actions, and Join Pile should be assigned only when a player enters the pile after the initial recovery attempt. Ball Carry applies only when a player clearly possesses the ball and advances after a clean recovery. Either the receiving team or kicking team may ultimately secure the ball. Pileups may obscure possession, and legal touching or the exact recovery distance may be difficult to determine from some All-22 or broadcast camera angles; when possession or eligibility is not visually confirmable, annotate only the observable movement and contact.

OutAndUp.definition: A vertical double-move pass concept in which the primary receiver releases upfield, breaks toward the sideline to sell a standard out route, then plants and redirects vertically along the boundary. The route is designed to make the defender drive toward the out break or surrender vertical leverage before the receiver accelerates upfield for a deep pass.
observable_cues: Primary receiver aligns outside or with enough width to threaten an out route toward the sideline
Primary receiver releases vertically and pushes the defender upfield
Primary receiver makes a sharp outside break toward the sideline
Primary receiver briefly flattens toward the sideline as if completing a standard out route
Primary receiver may turn the shoulders or head toward the quarterback during the out-route fake
Primary receiver plants the outside foot and redirects vertically after selling the out route
Primary receiver accelerates upfield along the sideline after the second break
Defender may drive toward the sideline, open the hips toward the out route, or lose vertical leverage
QB executes a pass drop and holds the ball long enough for the double move to develop
QB may pump fake toward the apparent out route before resetting to throw deep
QB resets, steps up, or repositions in the pocket before throwing toward the primary receiver
Offensive line uses sustained pass sets and pass protection for the developing vertical route
RB checks protection before blocking, releasing into a checkdown, or occupying an underneath defender
Complementary receivers run clear-out, seam, underneath, or backside routes to control coverage
OutAndUp.notes: The defining sequence is the primary receiver's vertical stem, clear outside break, convincing out-route presentation, plant-and-redirect, and renewed vertical acceleration along the sideline. Turn To Quarterback, Flatten To Sideline, and Pump Fake strengthen the deception but may not be visible in every clip. Track Ball, Catch Pass, and Run After Catch are optional outcomes and should not be required for classification. Do not label a standard out route, corner route, fade, comeback, straight go route, Stop and Go, or Slant and Go as Out and Up unless the receiver clearly sells an outside out route before redirecting vertically.

OutRoutes.definition: A sideline-breaking pass concept in which the primary receiver releases vertically, gains a defined route depth, decelerates at the top of the route, and plants before breaking sharply toward the nearest sideline. After the break, the receiver flattens the route horizontally or slightly downhill, turns toward the quarterback, and presents an outside target timed with the quarterback's throw.
observable_cues: Primary out receiver aligns outside, in the slot, in a reduced split, or within a stacked formation
Primary out receiver releases vertically or slightly inside immediately after the snap
Primary out receiver maintains a vertical stem toward a defined route break point
Primary out receiver gains measurable route depth before redirecting toward the sideline
Primary out receiver decelerates near the top of the route
Primary out receiver sinks the hips and plants before changing direction
Primary out receiver breaks sharply toward the nearest sideline
Receiver's route path becomes horizontal or slightly downhill after the outside break
Receiver turns the head and upper body toward the quarterback while continuing outside
Receiver maintains usable space between the route path and the sideline
QB uses a quick, intermediate, or deeper pass drop based on the route depth
QB sets the feet and prepares to throw before or shortly after the receiver breaks outside
QB releases the ball toward the outside route window with anticipation
Offensive line sustains pass protection until the receiver reaches the break point
Complementary receivers use vertical, flat, inside, or clear-out routes to create sideline space
OutRoutes.notes: The defining sequence is a meaningful vertical stem, a visible deceleration and hip sink at the break point, a planted change of direction toward the nearest sideline, and a flattened outside route path. Route depth may vary: a short stem may represent a quick-out variation, while a longer stem may represent an intermediate or deep-out variation. The general Out Route classification remains valid when the stem, plant, outside break, and sideline path are visible. Speed-out variations may show less pronounced deceleration or hip sink but must still include a clear transition from vertical movement to an outside-breaking path. Track Ball, Catch Pass, Secure Catch, Toe Tap, Turn Upfield, and Run After Catch are optional outcomes. Do not classify a flat route, corner route, comeback route, hitch route, or out-and-up route as Out Route unless the receiver clearly gains route depth and establishes a sustained path toward the nearest sideline.

OutsideZoneRead.definition: A zone stretch run where the quarterback reads the unblocked edge defender to decide to hand off to the running back or keep the ball, stretching the defense horizontally to create cutback lanes.
observable_cues: Offensive line zone-steps to playside
Quarterback in shotgun with RB offset
Tight end shading outside pre-snap
At snap: QB eyes edge defender movement
RB flows laterally to edge seeking seam
OutsideZoneRead.notes: Effective against aggressive defenses that overcommit to the edge; relies on precise QB read; can yield big gains if defender misleads; vulnerable to backside pursuit if seal blocks fail.

OutsideZoneStretch.definition: A wide zone run designed to horizontally stretch the defensive front through coordinated lateral movement by the offensive line. Covered linemen attempt to reach or overtake play-side defenders, while uncovered linemen assist on combination blocks before climbing to linebackers. The running back takes a wide track toward an outside landmark, presses the edge, reads the leverage of the edge defender and interior pursuit, and then chooses to bounce outside, bend vertically through a crease, or cut back behind over-pursuing defenders. The base concept normally uses a conventional handoff, does not intentionally leave an edge defender unblocked for the quarterback to read, and does not require a pulling offensive lineman.
observable_cues: Entire offensive line takes coordinated lateral or bucket steps toward the play side
Offensive linemen work to reach or overtake the play-side shoulder of defenders
Line of scrimmage appears to move horizontally toward the play-side sideline
Adjacent offensive linemen execute combination blocks while moving laterally
One blocker leaves a combination block to climb to a linebacker
Backside offensive linemen work across defenders to cut off pursuit
No guard or tackle pulls across the formation in the base version
Tight end reaches, widens, or seals the edge defender
RB takes a wide initial track toward the outside leg of the tight end or another perimeter landmark
RB keeps the shoulders relatively square while pressing the outside track
RB remains patient behind the laterally moving offensive line before making the final cut
RB reads the leverage of the first down defender outside the play-side tackle or tight end
RB may bounce outside when the edge is secured
RB may plant and bend vertically through a developing crease
RB may cut back behind defenders flowing aggressively toward the play side
Defensive pursuit stretches laterally and may create a backside cutback lane
QB completes a conventional handoff without visibly reading an intentionally unblocked edge defender
OutsideZoneStretch.notes: Outside Zone Stretch is distinguished from Inside Zone by greater lateral offensive-line displacement and a wider RB track toward an outside landmark; Inside Zone is more vertically oriented and usually attacks interior gaps earlier. Unlike Outside Zone Read, Outside Zone Stretch normally uses a conventional handoff and does not intentionally leave an edge defender unblocked for the QB to read; a backside cutoff assignment should not automatically be labeled as a read defender. Unlike Toss Sweep, the ball is normally handed off rather than tossed or pitched, and the RB initially presses behind the offensive line instead of immediately racing to the perimeter. Unlike Pin and Pull, Outside Zone Stretch relies on coordinated zone steps and reach blocks rather than down blocks and pulling linemen. Unlike Power or Counter, the base concept normally has no pulling guard and creates horizontal stretch rather than a predetermined downhill gap. The exact aiming point, reach-block combinations, and second-level assignments change according to the formation and defensive front.

PinAndPull.definition: The Pin & Pull is a gap scheme run play where offensive linemen to the play-side 'pin' (block down on) interior defenders, while other linemen 'pull' (move horizontally along the line of scrimmage) to lead the ball carrier around the perimeter, creating an outside running lane.
observable_cues: Playside OG pins defensive lineman inside
Backside OG pulls across formation to lead on second level
Backside OT down-blocks defensive end
RB widens and follows pulling guard to edge
QB executes inside fake before handoff
PinAndPull.notes: The Pin & Pull is an outside run where offensive linemen execute immediate down blocks ('pins') while others pull to lead the ball carrier around the perimeter. In contrast, the Counter is a gap scheme that utilizes misdirection, often involving a false step by the running back and/or initial movement by pulling linemen away from the intended point of attack, before hitting an inside or tight outside lane. While both use pulling linemen, the Pin & Pull aims for direct perimeter attack, whereas the Counter relies on deception to displace defenders before striking.

Post10to15.definition: A deep passing concept in which the primary receiver releases vertically, threatens a go route, and then plants at intermediate or deep route depth before breaking diagonally toward the middle of the field or goalpost. The receiver accelerates through the inside break while the quarterback reads the deep coverage and delivers the ball into the middle-field window.
observable_cues: Primary receiver aligns outside, in the slot, or as an attached receiving threat with room to attack the middle of the field
Primary receiver releases vertically and initially threatens a go route
Primary receiver maintains a sustained vertical stem before making the route break
Primary receiver may adjust the stem to attack the defender's leverage
Primary receiver plants at intermediate or deep route depth
Primary receiver breaks diagonally toward the middle of the field or goalpost
Primary receiver accelerates through the inside break rather than stopping or settling
Primary receiver crosses into space between or behind deep defenders
QB executes a pass drop and remains in the pocket while the route develops
QB directs attention toward the deep coverage before throwing into the post-route window
QB may step up or reposition within the pocket before delivering the pass
Offensive line uses sustained pass sets and pass protection for the developing downfield route
RB checks protection before blocking, releasing into a checkdown, or occupying an underneath defender
Complementary receivers run vertical, clear-out, underneath, or backside routes that occupy safeties and clear the middle
Post10to15.notes: The defining sequence is the primary receiver's vertical release, sustained vertical stem, plant at route depth, diagonal break toward the middle, and acceleration through the break. Track Ball, Catch Pass, Secure Catch, and Run After Catch are optional outcomes and should not be required for classification. Step Up In Pocket may occur but is not required. Do not label a go route, corner route, deep dig, slant, or skinny post as a standard Post unless the receiver clearly stems vertically before making a deep diagonal inside break. The route depth and break angle may vary based on coverage, field position, receiver alignment, and coaching terminology.

Power.definition: A downhill gap-scheme run built around play-side down blocks, a backside guard pulling across the formation to lead through the point of attack, and an edge blocker kicking out or sealing the force defender. The down blocks and kick-out block create a structured inside-out running lane, typically through the play-side B-gap or C-gap. The running back takes a downhill track, follows the pulling guard, and makes a decisive cut inside or outside the kick-out block based on defender leverage. Base Power normally uses one puller, most commonly the backside guard, and is not defined by coordinated lateral zone movement or multiple vertical double teams across the entire offensive line.
observable_cues: Play-side offensive linemen take inside or down-block steps
Play-side blockers close interior gaps and prevent defensive penetration
Backside guard leaves the original alignment and pulls laterally behind the line of scrimmage
Pulling guard crosses the center's original alignment toward the play side
Pulling guard turns vertically through the designated B-gap or C-gap
Pulling guard leads through the hole to block a linebacker or second-level defender
Tight end, fullback, H-back, or play-side blocker kicks out or seals the force defender
A defined running lane forms between the play-side down blocks and the edge kick-out block
Backside tackle blocks down, hinges, or cuts off backside pursuit after the guard pulls
Center blocks back on a nose tackle or backside defensive tackle when required by the defensive front
RB takes a downhill track toward the play-side B-gap or C-gap
RB remains behind the pulling guard before entering the point of attack
RB follows the pulling guard through the designated gap
RB may cut inside the kick-out block when the edge defender is widened
RB may bounce outside when the edge defender wrong-arms the kick-out block and is sealed inside
Offensive-line movement is primarily angular and vertical rather than coordinated lateral zone movement
Only one primary pulling offensive lineman is normally visible in the base version
Ball is handed to the RB without a counter-direction false step in the base version
Power.notes: Power is distinguished from Counter by the RB's direct path toward the play side without a counter step or initial movement away from the point of attack; traditional Counter also commonly uses two backfield blockers or two pullers, while base Power normally uses one pulling guard and a stationary kick-out blocker. Unlike Duo, Power has a clearly observable pulling guard, while Duo normally relies on multiple vertical double teams with no puller and an RB reading a linebacker. Unlike Iso, Power uses the pulling guard as the primary lead blocker, while Iso normally uses a fullback to isolate a linebacker. Unlike Trap, the Power puller generally leads through the hole to block a linebacker rather than trapping an initially unblocked interior defensive lineman. Unlike Inside Zone, Power uses down blocks, a defined point of attack, and a pulling guard instead of coordinated zone rules. Unlike Pin and Pull, Power usually sends one backside guard through an interior or off-tackle gap rather than using multiple pullers around the perimeter. The identity of the kick-out blocker may vary among the TE, FB, H-back, or another surface blocker, but the combination of play-side down blocks, a backside guard pull, an edge kick-out or seal, and the RB following the puller remains the defining visual structure.

PuntBlock.definition: An aggressive punt-rush play in which one or more receiving-team players attack the punt protection immediately after the snap with the intent to reach the punter and contact the football during the kicking operation. Rushers may attack an edge, interior gap, overload, stunt, or delayed lane, while other players contain a fake, occupy protectors, maintain a return option, or prepare to recover a blocked or deflected ball.
observable_cues: Receiving team crowds the line of scrimmage or places multiple players in clear rush positions
Rushers align in narrow, edge, overloaded, stacked, or staggered positions before the snap
Designated rushers move immediately toward the punt protection at the snap
Rushers attack specific interior gaps, edges, or the punter's anticipated launch point
Rushers attempt to avoid, split, cross, or defeat punt-protection blocks
One or more rushers continue accelerating toward the punter instead of retreating to establish a return
Primary rusher bends toward the punter after clearing the protection
Primary rusher extends the arms, leaves the feet, or crosses the punter's kicking lane
Punter receives the long snap and begins the normal catch, set, approach, and kicking operation
Punt-team protectors maintain firm protection sets instead of immediately releasing into coverage
Contact with the football may occur during or immediately after the punter's kicking motion
A blocked punt may show a shortened flight, altered trajectory, backward deflection, or loose ball near the line of scrimmage
Nearby players locate and move toward the football after a block or deflection
Returner may remain deep as a secondary option or move forward after recognizing the blocked punt
One or more receiving-team players maintain edge responsibility against a fake punt
PuntBlock.notes: The defining sequence is an immediate committed rush after the snap, penetration through or around the punt protection, closure toward the punter's launch point, and an observable attempt to contact the football. Extend To Block and Dive To Block may occur but are not required. Block Punt is a successful outcome and should not be required for classification. Locate Ball, Attempt Recovery, Secure Recovery, and Advance Ball apply only when the punt is blocked, deflected, mishandled, or remains loose. Do not classify a standard punt return, punt-safe call, fair-catch return, or late coverage collision as Punt Block unless the receiving team shows a clear intentional rush toward the kicking point.

PuntCoverage.definition: A special-teams play in which the punting team executes a punt and releases coverage players downfield in coordinated lanes to maintain leverage, locate the returner, close available return paths, and tackle the returner or control the ball near its landing point.
observable_cues: Punting team aligns with a long snapper, punter, personal protector, interior protectors, gunners, and coverage players
Return team aligns with one or more deep returners and players positioned to rush the punt or delay coverage releases
Long snap travels from the snapper to the punter
Punter receives and controls the snap before beginning the punt approach
Interior protectors engage or position against rushers before releasing downfield
Punter drops and strikes the football with the foot
Gunners release rapidly near the sidelines and attempt to defeat vice-player hold-up techniques
Interior coverage players transition from punt protection into downfield coverage
Coverage players spread across the field with visible spacing between adjacent lanes
Outside coverage players maintain leverage outside the returner
Interior coverage players close from inside-out toward the return path
Coverage players track the punt while locating the returner
Coverage players adjust their pursuit angles after the ball is caught, collected, or allowed to bounce
Coverage players avoid unnecessary lane crossings and attempt to prevent an open return crease
Returner may signal for a fair catch, catch and advance the punt, collect a bouncing ball, or allow the ball to continue rolling
One or more coverage players close the return lane while additional players maintain surrounding leverage
Coverage players break down before attempting controlled contact
Coverage players attempt to tackle, force the returner out of bounds, or surround the returner
Secondary coverage players continue pursuit after a missed tackle
Coverage players may touch, stop, or down an unreturned punt near its resting point
Multiple coverage players converge around the ball or returner near the end of the play
Play ends with a tackle, out-of-bounds result, fair catch, downed punt, touchback, whistle, or official signal
PuntCoverage.notes: Punt coverage may use lane, directional, contain, net-punt, or gunner-pressure principles from shield, spread, or directional punt formations. Punt trajectories may include high-hang-time, directional, line-drive, end-over-end, and bouncing punts. Teams may use single or double gunners, and those gunners may release cleanly, be held up, be double-teamed, avoid contact, or be forced toward the sideline. Interior protectors may delay their coverage release when facing immediate punt pressure, and coverage players may exchange, overlap, or temporarily leave their apparent lanes as the return develops. Maintain Coverage Lane should be based on visible spacing and movement rather than an inferred assignment. Release Downfield begins only when a player visibly transitions from protection or the initial alignment into coverage movement. Locate Returner identifies a visible change in attention or body orientation toward the returner, while Pursue Returner begins when the player runs toward the identified ball carrier. Break Down should be separated from Attempt Tackle, and proximity alone is not a tackle attempt. Secure Tackle requires the player to control and stop the returner, while Miss Tackle requires a visible failed tackle attempt. Join Tackle applies only when a second or subsequent player enters an existing tackle. Down Punt requires a visible action that intentionally stops or controls an unreturned punt; merely standing near a stopped ball is insufficient. Touch Ball identifies visible contact without clear control. Coverage outcomes may include a tackle, force out of bounds, fair catch, downed punt, touchback, muff, or no return. Tackles may be made by a gunner, contain player, interior coverage player, long snapper, personal protector, or punter. Missed tackles may lead to secondary pursuit and additional tackle attempts. Penalties such as holding, illegal blocks, return interference, or illegal touching may not be visible or enforced within the clip. Camera views may temporarily lose the ball, returner, gunners, or outside coverage lanes, and congestion may make the first player to touch or control the ball difficult to identify. Punt Coverage should be distinguished from Punt Return, Punt Return Touchdown, Fair Catch, Downed Punt, Touchback, Blocked Punt, Fake Punt, and Muffed Punt Recovery. Recognition should require visible downfield coverage behavior after a normal punt rather than punt formation, snap, kick, or a single gunner release alone.

PuntReturnTouchdown.definition: A special-teams scoring play in which the receiving team fields a punt, establishes possession, executes a coordinated punt-return and blocking scheme, and advances the ball into the opponent's end zone while maintaining control.
observable_cues: Punting team aligns in a punt formation with a long snapper, punter, protectors, gunners, and interior coverage players
Return team aligns with a deep returner and players assigned to rush, hold up, or block coverage players
Long snap travels from the snapper to the punter
Punter receives the snap, approaches the ball, and punts it downfield
Gunners and other coverage players release downfield after the punt
Returner tracks the punt and adjusts position beneath or toward the projected landing point
Returner does not visibly signal for a fair catch before attempting the return
Returner catches the airborne punt or collects a bouncing, rolling, or loose ball
Returner secures the ball against the hands, arm, chest, or body before advancing
Vice players engage, mirror, double-team, or delay outside gunners
Interior return-team players identify and block approaching coverage players
Return-team blockers establish a middle, boundary, field, wall, or cross-field return lane
Returner presses the designed return lane while reading the developing blocks
Returner follows blockers and accelerates through an available crease
Returner makes one or more cuts or changes direction to avoid defenders
Returner may reverse field when the initial return lane closes
Returner breaks, slips, or avoids tackle attempts while maintaining balance and possession
Lead blockers advance ahead of or beside the returner
Coverage players pursue from inside-out, outside-in, or from behind
Outside coverage players attempt to maintain contain and prevent a reversal
Returner reaches open field and continues advancing toward the opponent's end zone
Teammates escort the returner and remain available to block pursuing defenders
Returner visibly crosses the opponent's goal line while controlling the ball
Visible end-zone possession, an official touchdown signal, or other reliable scoring evidence confirms the result
Play ends after the touchdown, official signal, celebration, or whistle
PuntReturnTouchdown.notes: Punt return touchdowns may develop from middle, boundary, field, wall, cross-field, or double-team gunner return schemes and may occur against directional, high-hang-time, line-drive, end-over-end, or bouncing punts. Catch Punt applies only when the returner cleanly receives an airborne punt before it contacts the ground, while Collect Ball applies when possession is gained from a bouncing, rolling, muffed, or loose punt. Touching, bobbling, or briefly contacting the ball does not establish possession. Secure Ball requires visible control against the hands, arm, chest, or body, and Ball Carry begins only when the player advances with possession. Signal Fair Catch should be assigned only when the returner visibly raises and waves one arm above the head before the catch; a valid fair-catch sequence should not be classified as a punt return touchdown without clear evidence of an unusual continuation and a score. Double Team Gunner requires two return-team players coordinating against one gunner, while Hold Up Gunner may be performed by a single vice player who engages, mirrors, or delays the release. Press Return Lane identifies the returner's initial attack of the designed path, Follow Block identifies movement behind a blocker using that block's leverage, Cut To Lane identifies a plant and redirection into an available crease, and Reverse Field requires movement across a substantial portion of the field after the original path closes. Break Tackle requires meaningful defender contact followed by continued advancement, while Avoid Tackle applies when the returner evades the attempt without being significantly controlled. Miss Tackle should be assigned only when an observable tackle attempt fails. Variations may include single-returner or two-returner formations, multiple cuts, reversals of field, laterals, handoffs, a muff followed by recovery and advancement, or a punt touched first by the kicking team. Cross Goal Line requires the ball carrier to visibly cross the opponent's goal line while maintaining control, and Touchdown requires reliable scoring evidence such as visible end-zone entry, continued possession in the end zone, an official signal, or connected scoreboard evidence. Significant return yardage, celebration, reduced pursuit, the returner leaving the camera view, or the clip ending near the goal line is not sufficient by itself. Penalties may nullify an apparent touchdown without being visible in the clip, and some camera views may temporarily lose the ball or returner, making possession or the exact goal-line crossing frame uncertain. A true punt return touchdown must be distinguished from a fair catch, downed punt, touchback, standard punt return, blocked-punt touchdown, muffed-punt recovery touchdown, or another loose-ball recovery score.

QuickScreens.definition: A quick perimeter passing concept in which the quarterback receives the snap, immediately turns or sets toward a designated receiver near the line of scrimmage, and delivers the ball before a normal downfield route can develop. The screen receiver moves laterally, retreats slightly, or remains near the original alignment while nearby eligible receivers establish immediate perimeter blocks, allowing the receiver to catch the pass in space and run behind the blocking structure.
observable_cues: Screen receiver aligns outside, in the slot, within a bunch, or near the perimeter before the snap
QB immediately turns the shoulders, hips, or feet toward the screen side after receiving the snap
QB uses a catch-and-throw action, quick set, or minimal pass drop
Screen receiver moves laterally, retreats slightly, or remains near the original alignment
Screen receiver turns toward the quarterback almost immediately after the snap
Screen receiver settles near or behind the line of scrimmage without using a prolonged vertical route stem
QB releases the pass before a standard downfield route has time to develop
Nearby eligible receivers immediately locate and engage perimeter defenders
Blocking receivers position themselves outside, inside, or directly in front of the screen receiver
TE or RB may move into a lead-blocking position on the perimeter
Offensive linemen use brief pass sets, cutoff blocks, or pursuit-control blocks near the line of scrimmage
Offensive linemen generally remain near the line rather than releasing far downfield
Screen receiver catches or attempts to catch the pass near or behind the line of scrimmage
Screen receiver follows the developing blockers, reads the blocking leverage, or selects a perimeter running lane
The play lacks the prolonged route sell, hold, and delayed return associated with a WR Slow Screen
QuickScreens.notes: The defining sequence is the quarterback's immediate orientation and short throw toward a receiver near the line of scrimmage, combined with the receiver's immediate availability and a visible perimeter blocking structure. The screen receiver may use Lateral Release, Retreat For Screen, or remain near the original alignment, so no single release variation is required. Catch Pass, Secure Catch, Follow Blockers, Read Block, Cut To Lane, Accelerate Upfield, and Run After Catch are optional outcomes and should not be required for classification. Do not label a WR Slow Screen, bubble screen, tunnel screen, running back screen, or standard quick pass as Quick Screens unless the immediate short throw and screen-blocking structure are both reasonably visible.

RPO.definition: A post-snap option concept that combines a called run with one or more attached quick-pass routes. The quarterback receives the snap, establishes a mesh with the running back, reads a designated conflict defender, and either completes the handoff or pulls the ball and throws immediately to an attached receiver. The offensive line executes the called run-blocking scheme on both branches while the run and pass elements develop simultaneously.
RPO.protection_scheme: Run Blocking With Attached Pass Option
observable_cues: Offense aligns in shotgun or pistol with the running back positioned to cross the quarterback's mesh point
One or more receivers align to execute an attached quick route or screen
QB receives the snap and extends the ball toward the running back
QB and RB establish a visible mesh or extended handoff presentation
QB directs the helmet, shoulders, or attention toward a second-level or perimeter read defender during or immediately after the mesh
QB either completes the handoff or pulls the ball before the running back secures possession
Offensive line fires forward or laterally using run-blocking footwork instead of conventional pass sets
At least one receiver releases immediately into a slant, glance, hitch, bubble, flat, stick, quick out, or screen route
Run blocking and attached route development occur at the same time
RB continues along the called run track even when the quarterback pulls the ball
When the pass branch is selected, QB sets and throws immediately after the pull
The pass is delivered near or shortly beyond the line of scrimmage before the run-blocking line advances too far downfield
When the run branch is selected, RB secures the handoff and presses the called run path
The play lacks the prolonged run fake, pass-set transition, and deeper quarterback drop associated with play action
RPO.notes: The defining structure is a real quarterback-running back mesh, simultaneous run blocking by the offensive line, an attached quick route or screen, and a post-snap give-or-pull decision by the quarterback. Give Handoff and Pull Ball are mutually exclusive outcomes. Set To Throw and Throw Pass occur only on the pass branch, while Take Handoff and Ball Carry occur only on the run branch. The specific offensive-line action may be Zone Block, Reach Block, Combo Block, Down Block, or another run-scheme action, so Zone Block should be interpreted as representative rather than universally required. Classification confidence should be highest when the mesh, run blocking, attached route, visible quarterback read, give-or-pull decision, and immediate throw after a pull are all observable. Track Ball, Catch Pass, Secure Catch, Turn Upfield, and Run After Catch are optional outcomes. Do not classify a standard handoff, play-action pass, zone read quarterback keep, packaged pre-snap throw, quick screen, or conventional dropback pass as RPO unless the simultaneous mesh, post-snap read, run blocking, and attached pass option are reasonably visible.

Sack.definition: A defensive play result in which the quarterback begins or remains in a passing posture, retains possession of the football, and is contacted and controlled by one or more defenders behind the line of scrimmage before completing a forward pass. The quarterback may be wrapped and brought to the ground, tripped, driven backward, forced out of bounds, or ruled down while under defensive control. The defining observable sequence is defensive access to the quarterback followed by contact, control, and termination of the play behind the line of scrimmage.
Sack.rush_structure: A sack may be produced by an individual pass rusher, a coordinated four-man rush, an interior or edge pressure, a linebacker or defensive-back blitz, or multiple defenders compressing the pocket together. Edge rushers attack the offensive tackles while maintaining or closing outside escape lanes, and interior rushers attack pass-protection gaps to restrict the quarterback's ability to step forward. The sack defender may defeat a blocker, penetrate an open gap, arrive unblocked, loop into a different rush lane, or pursue the quarterback after the pocket breaks down. Other defenders may contribute by collapsing the pocket, maintaining contain, redirecting the quarterback, or sustaining coverage long enough for the primary rusher to finish the play.
observable_cues: Quarterback receives the snap and begins a pass drop, play-action setup, rollout, or passing progression
Defensive rushers show forward get-off toward the offensive backfield
Edge rushers attack outside or inside the offensive tackles
Interior rushers attack pass-protection gaps and restrict the quarterback's ability to step forward
A linebacker or defensive back may enter the rush as an immediate or delayed blitzer
Rushers engage, avoid, cross the face of, or work around pass blockers
A defender penetrates a gap or visibly separates from a blocker
The pocket compresses from the edge, interior, or both
The quarterback climbs, retreats, rolls out, resets, or attempts to escape while still possessing the ball
A contain defender limits the quarterback's outside escape path
A contributing rusher redirects the quarterback toward the sack defender
The sack defender closes the remaining distance to the quarterback
Initial contact occurs before the quarterback completes a forward pass
The sack defender wraps, grabs, trips, drives, or otherwise controls the quarterback
The quarterback is brought down, forced out of bounds, or ruled down behind the line of scrimmage
The play ends with the quarterback still possessing the football unless a clearly visible strip-sack occurs
A second defender may join the tackle and contribute to an assisted or shared sack
Sack.notes: A sack requires observable pass intent or a continued passing posture, quarterback possession, defensive contact or control, and termination of the play behind the line of scrimmage before a completed forward pass. Do not classify a pressure, hurry, post-release quarterback hit, tackle after a completed pass, or tackle on a designed quarterback run as a sack. A quarterback who begins with pass intent may still be sacked while scrambling if controlled before reaching or crossing the line of scrimmage. The sack defender does not need to engage or shed a blocker when arriving unblocked. Assign Assist Sack only when a second defender visibly contributes to controlling or bringing down the quarterback. Include Force Fumble or Recover Fumble only when the corresponding event is clearly visible. Because no specific clip evidence is provided in this definition, named blitzes, exact rush moves, official sack credit, and clip-specific defender roles should be assigned only during video annotation.

SlantAndGo.definition: A vertical double-move pass concept in which the primary receiver releases upfield, sells an inside slant break, then plants and redirects vertically to create separation from a defender who reacts to the initial inside movement. The quarterback times a deep throw after the receiver transitions back upfield, while complementary routes occupy underneath and deep coverage defenders.
observable_cues: Primary receiver aligns outside or with enough space to threaten both the slant and vertical route
Primary receiver releases vertically and pushes the defender upfield
Primary receiver sharply leans, steps, or breaks toward the inside as if running a slant
Primary receiver plants the inside foot and redirects vertically after selling the slant
Primary receiver accelerates upfield after the second break
Defender may drive toward the inside break before turning to recover vertically
QB executes a pass drop and holds the ball long enough for the double move to develop
QB may use a pump fake toward the slant window before resetting for the deep throw
QB sets or steps up in the pocket before throwing downfield toward the primary receiver
Offensive line uses sustained pass sets and pass protection for the developing vertical route
RB checks protection before blocking, releasing into a checkdown, or occupying an underneath defender
Complementary receivers run clear-out, seam, underneath, or backside routes to control safety help
SlantAndGo.notes: The defining sequence is the primary receiver's vertical stem, convincing inside slant sell, plant-and-redirect, and renewed vertical acceleration. A pump fake can strengthen the concept but is not required when it is not clearly visible. Track Ball, Catch Pass, and Run After Catch are optional outcomes and should not be required for classification. Do not label a standard slant, fade, post, or straight go route as Slant and Go unless the receiver clearly shows an inside slant fake followed by a vertical redirection.

Slants0to10.definition: A quick-game passing concept in which two or more eligible receivers release vertically for a short distance before planting and breaking diagonally toward the middle of the field. The slant routes are spaced or layered to create separate inside throwing windows, while the quarterback uses a quick drop or catch-and-throw rhythm to deliver the ball shortly after one receiver makes the inside break.
observable_cues: Two or more eligible receivers align with enough horizontal spacing to run inside-breaking routes
Multiple receivers release vertically or slightly outside immediately after the snap
Slant receivers use short vertical stems before making their route breaks
Multiple receivers plant and break diagonally toward the middle of the field
Inside-breaking routes develop simultaneously or in a closely timed sequence
Slant receivers maintain visible horizontal separation or staggered route depths
Primary slant receiver may attack the leverage of the nearest defender before breaking inside
Secondary slant receiver enters a separate inside passing lane from the primary receiver
QB executes a quick pass drop, short set, or catch-and-throw action
QB releases the ball shortly after one receiver makes the inside break
Offensive line uses quick pass sets and maintains short-duration pass protection
RB checks protection before blocking, releasing to the flat, or providing a checkdown option
Complementary receivers run flat, clear-out, backside, or underneath routes to stretch nearby defenders and open inside space
Slants0to10.notes: The defining sequence is two or more receivers using short vertical stems followed by planted diagonal inside breaks into separate passing lanes. At least two receivers must display slant-route behavior for classification as the Slants concept rather than an isolated slant. Settle In Zone may occur as a coverage adjustment but is not required. Track Ball, Catch Pass, Secure Catch, Turn Upfield, and Run After Catch are optional outcomes and should not be required for classification. Do not label a glance route, shallow cross, deep dig, spacing concept, quick hitch, or single slant as Slants unless multiple receivers clearly execute short inside-breaking route paths.

StopAndGo.definition: A vertical double-move pass concept in which the primary receiver releases upfield, decelerates and presents a stop, hitch, or curl route, then plants and redirects vertically. The route is designed to make the defender stop, squat, or drive toward the apparent short route before the receiver accelerates past the defender for a deep pass.
observable_cues: Primary receiver aligns outside or with enough space to threaten both a short stop route and a vertical route
Primary receiver releases vertically and pushes the defender upfield
Primary receiver visibly reduces speed after the initial vertical stem
Primary receiver sinks the hips, turns the shoulders, or presents the hands as if expecting a short pass
Primary receiver briefly stops, settles, or looks back toward the quarterback
Primary receiver plants and redirects vertically after selling the stop route
Primary receiver accelerates upfield after the second movement
Defender may stop, drive forward, or lose vertical leverage in reaction to the short-route fake
QB executes a pass drop and holds the ball long enough for the double move to develop
QB may pump fake toward the apparent stop route before resetting to throw deep
QB resets, steps up, or repositions in the pocket before throwing toward the primary receiver
Offensive line uses sustained pass sets and pass protection for the developing vertical route
RB checks protection before blocking, releasing into a checkdown, or occupying an underneath defender
Complementary receivers run clear-out, underneath, seam, or backside routes to control coverage
StopAndGo.notes: The defining sequence is the primary receiver's vertical stem, visible deceleration, convincing stop-route presentation, plant-and-redirect, and renewed vertical acceleration. Sink Hips, Turn To Quarterback, Settle, and Pump Fake strengthen the deception but may not be visible in every clip. Track Ball, Catch Pass, and Run After Catch are optional outcomes and should not be required for classification. Do not label a standard hitch, curl, comeback, fade, straight go route, or Slant and Go as Stop and Go unless the receiver clearly sells a stop-type route before redirecting vertically.

WRSlowScreens.definition: A delayed wide receiver screen in which the designated receiver initially releases upfield to sell a normal route, pauses or delays, then turns back toward the quarterback and settles near or behind the line of scrimmage. The quarterback briefly holds the ball or executes a controlled drop to draw defenders upfield before delivering a short pass, while receivers, tight ends, running backs, or offensive linemen release into space and form blocks in front of the receiver.
observable_cues: Screen receiver aligns outside, in the slot, or within a receiver cluster near the intended screen side
Screen receiver initially releases or stems vertically to sell a normal route
Screen receiver visibly delays before turning back toward the quarterback
Screen receiver returns toward or settles near or behind the line of scrimmage
QB executes a controlled pass drop or briefly holds the ball instead of throwing immediately after the snap
QB may set, retreat, or drift away from pressure to establish screen timing and a clear throwing lane
QB delivers a short pass toward the delayed screen receiver
Play-side blockers initially engage, pass-set, or delay before releasing toward the screen
Releasing offensive linemen move toward the perimeter or second level instead of sustaining normal pass protection
Blocking receivers delay before locating and engaging perimeter defenders
Screen receiver catches the pass behind or inside the developing blocking structure
Screen receiver follows the blockers before selecting a running lane
Screen receiver may cut inside, bounce outside, or accelerate upfield after the blocks develop
The pass and blocking structure develop more slowly than a smoke screen, bubble screen, or immediate perimeter screen
WRSlowScreens.notes: The defining sequence is the screen receiver's initial route sell, deliberate delay, turn back toward the quarterback, and settlement near or behind the line of scrimmage, combined with a delayed short pass and blockers releasing into screen position. Catch Pass and Follow Blockers usually confirm the design when the pass is completed, but a completion, successful block, or long gain is not required for classification. Do not label an immediate smoke screen, laterally expanding bubble screen, inside-developing tunnel screen, or standard downfield route as WR Slow Screen unless the receiver clearly delays after selling an initial route.
